Den
den
n. (rendering Hebrew me'ōnah/gob, Greek spēlaion)
From Saxon denn, a cave or lair of a beast. The word keeps its animal sense throughout Scripture: a den is where a predator lives and where it drags what it has taken, which is why the Lord's use of it for the temple courts is so severe.

Biblical Definition

A den is a lair, and Scripture uses it for the places where dangerous things are at home. Daniel's trial is the plainest: “Then the king commanded, and they brought Daniel, and cast him into the den of lions” (Daniel 6:16) — a man condemned by a law framed against his prayers, delivered not from the den but in it. Jeremiah takes the same word for what the temple had become in the hands of men who sinned all week and sheltered in it on the sabbath: “Is this house, which is called by my name, become a den of robbers in your eyes?” (Jeremiah 7:11). Our Lord quotes that verse when He overturns the tables: “My house shall be called the house of prayer; but ye have made it a den of thieves” (Matthew 21:13). The charge is precise and worth hearing exactly. A den is not where thieves rob; it is where they retire after robbing, feeling safe. The accusation is not merely that the temple traffic was dishonest but that religion had become the hiding place of men who intended to keep their sin. And the last use is a promise that the lair itself will be harmless: “the weaned child shall put his hand on the cockatrice' den” (Isaiah 11:8) — a world under Messiah's reign where a child may reach into the place of death and take no hurt.

Webster 1828 Definition

A cave or hollow place; the lair of a wild beast. In Scripture, the den of lions into which Daniel was cast, the temple made a den of robbers and of thieves, and the cockatrice' den on which a weaned child shall safely put his hand.

expand to see more

DEN, n. 1. A cave or hollow place in the earth; usually the retreat of a wild beast.

2. Any squalid or wretched place of resort.

3. A place of retreat and security for men of evil design; as, a den of thieves.

4. From Saxon denn, a cave, a lair.

5. In Scripture, cast him into the den of lions, Dan. 6; ye have made it a den of thieves, Matt. 21.

Key Scripture

Daniel 6:16 — "Then the king commanded, and they brought Daniel, and cast him into the den of lions. Now the king spake and said unto Daniel, Thy God whom thou servest continually, he will deliver thee."

Jeremiah 7:11 — "Is this house, which is called by my name, become a den of robbers in your eyes? Behold, even I have seen it, saith the LORD."

Matthew 21:13 — "And said unto them, It is written, My house shall be called the house of prayer; but ye have made it a den of thieves."

Isaiah 11:8 — "And the sucking child shall play on the hole of the asp, and the weaned child shall put his hand on the cockatrice' den."

Modern Corruption

The cleansing of the temple is reduced to a protest against commerce or unjust pricing, missing the charge Christ actually made — that the house of prayer had become the refuge of unrepentant men.

expand to see more

The temple cleansing is now most often preached as an economic protest: the money changers overcharged, the poor were exploited, and Christ acted for the marginalised. Exploitation there certainly was, and Scripture never excuses it. But the verse He quoted supplies the actual indictment, and Jeremiah 7 leaves no ambiguity about it. The prophet lists the sins — stealing, murder, adultery, false swearing, burning incense unto Baal — and then says the people came and stood before God in His house and said, We are delivered to do all these abominations. That is a den: a place where predators feel safe. The Lord's charge against the temple traffic is that religion had been converted into cover, and the cover is what enraged Him. Any church that offers men assurance without repentance is running the same establishment with better music.

Daniel's den corrects a different modern instinct, which reads deliverance as escape from trouble. Daniel was not spared the den; he was put into it, and God shut the lions' mouths while he was inside. The distinction matters pastorally, because most believers are not delivered from their trials but kept through them. The king's decree had been framed precisely to catch a man who prayed, and Daniel went home and prayed with his windows open toward Jerusalem as he did aforetime — the whole strength of the account lying in that phrase, as he did aforetime. He did not increase his devotion to meet the crisis or reduce it to survive; he continued. The principle to recover is that faithfulness before the test is what carries a man through it.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew me'ōnah, a lair or dwelling of beasts; Aramaic gob, a pit or den; Greek spēlaion, a cave used as a lair.

expand to see more

Hebrew me'ōnah (H4585) — a den or habitation, especially of lions; “the lion's den” (Nahum 2:12).

Aramaic gob (H1358) — a pit or den; the word used throughout Daniel 6 for the lions' den.

Hebrew me'arah (H4631) — a cave; the word Jeremiah uses for the den of robbers (Jeremiah 7:11).

Greek spēlaion (G4693) — a cave or den; “a den of thieves” (Matthew 21:13; Mark 11:17; Luke 19:46).

Greek lēstēs (G3027) — a robber or brigand, not a petty thief; the violent word behind “den of thieves.”

Usage

"Of preservation in the trial rather than from it: cast him into the den of lions (Daniel 6:16)."

"Of religion turned into cover for sin: Is this house... become a den of robbers in your eyes? (Jeremiah 7:11)."

"Of the peace of Messiah's reign: the weaned child shall put his hand on the cockatrice' den (Isaiah 11:8)."
